result: The minimal model with negative feedback from a slow storage mechanism recapitulates the main hallmarks of habituation including spontaneous recovery, potentiation, subliminal accumulation, and input sensitivity, as demonstrated through model simulations.
evaluation: All three reviewers affirm the model's ability to reproduce habituation hallmarks. Reviewer 1 states the evidence is 'solid, and uses simulations of the minimal model to recapitulate several hallmarks of habituation.' Reviewer 2 notes 'the model is simple enough to allow for some analytic understanding but at the same time exhibits most basic properties of habituation in sensory systems.' Reviewer 3 confirms 'the presence of three units (receptor, readout, storage) operating at different time scales and executing negative feedback can be found in many domains of biology.'

result: Information gain peaks at intermediate levels of habituation, revealing that optimal processing performance is associated with intermediate activity reduction, as both too-strong and too-weak negative feedback are detrimental to information gain.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly support this finding. Reviewer 2 states 'the author's finding of maximal information gain for intermediate habituation strength via an optimization principle is, in general, interesting.' Reviewer 3 highlights this as 'a key takeaway demonstrated by the authors that has wide relevance is that large information gain and large habituation cannot be attained simultaneously.' No concerns are raised about this core result.

result: The region of maximal information gain can be characterized through an optimal trade-off between information and energy consumption via Pareto optimization, and systems can spontaneously tune to this region, which corresponds to intermediate habituation with concurrent energetic advantage.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 raises significant concerns about the generality of this finding, asking 'How general is their finding that the optimal Pareto front coincides with the region of maximal information gain?' and requesting exploration of different parameter regimes and signal strengths. While Reviewer 3 notes 'parameter regimes that enable these properties also result in low dissipation,' the lack of response to Reviewer 2's specific questions about robustness leaves the generality of this optimization principle uncertain.

result: The model captures the main components of observed neural habituation in zebrafish larvae subjected to repeated looming stimulations, as demonstrated through comparison of PCA analysis between model predictions and experimental data.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 expresses skepticism about this comparison, stating 'The comparison to experimental data isn't very convincing.' They raise specific methodological concerns: 'is PCA performed simultaneously on both the experimental data set and on the model or separately? What are the units of the PCs in Fig. 6(b,c)? Given that the model parameters are chosen so that the activity decrease in the model is similar to the one in the data... isn't it expected that the dynamics in the PC1/2 space look very similar?' These unresolved questions indicate the experimental validation is not fully convincing.

result: The storage mechanism is fundamental to the model, playing the role of an effective memory that mediates negative feedback, and must evolve on a slower timescale comparable to the external input for habituation to occur.
evaluation: Reviewers affirm the importance of the storage mechanism. Reviewer 3 explicitly states 'A major strength of the work is the generality of the studied model. The presence of three units (receptor, readout, storage) operating at different time scales and executing negative feedback can be found in many domains of biology.' Reviewer 2 acknowledges the model features 'a slow memory variable that suppresses the receptor' without raising concerns about this architectural choice.

result: The functional advantages of habituation are rooted in the interplay between energy dissipation and information gain, suggesting habituation stems from an information-based advantage that sheds light on optimization principles underlying its emergence across biological scales.
evaluation: Reviewers support this conceptual conclusion. Reviewer 3 states 'When energetic considerations are accounted for, large information gain and intermediate habituation appear to be the favorable combination' and notes this has 'wide relevance.' Reviewer 1 describes the manuscript as 'valuable' and states 'The results here could be of use in interpreting habituation behavior in a range of biological systems,' affirming the broader implications of the information-theoretic framework.

result: The proposed model is intentionally minimal yet contains the essential ingredients for habituation to emerge naturally while remaining analytically tractable, serving as an archetypal description of sensing processes across biological scales.
evaluation: All reviewers affirm the model's appropriate level of abstraction. Reviewer 1 calls it 'a valuable minimal model.' Reviewer 2 states 'The author's simplified model serves as a good starting point for understanding habituation in different biological contexts as the model is simple enough to allow for some analytic understanding but at the same time exhibits most basic properties of habituation.' Reviewer 3 emphasizes 'A major strength of the work is the generality of the studied model.'
